clue.text: Book shortage not propitious?

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for book
a lack is a shortage

explanation.surface: A shortage of books is bad news for someone, perhaps a reader or a library.
explanation.definitionFit: A black outlook or black day is gloomy and unfavourable, the opposite of auspicious.

clue.text: Coastal locations — successful strikes taking out one

indicators.note: taking something out removes it, so a letter goes from the phrase before it

parts.note: big hits are successful strikes of the ball
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A list of coastal places alongside a tally of strikes, as if bombing targets or cricket shots.
explanation.walkthrough: BIG HITS loses its I to leave BIGHTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A bight is a curved bay or indentation in a coastline, so bights are features found along the shore.

clue.text: A newspaper comes with indication of alternative Northern member of fellowship

parts.note: taken as written
a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper
the word or introduces an alternative
N is the abbreviation for Northern

explanation.surface: A newspaper report that offers a choice of northern candidates for some society's membership.
explanation.walkthrough: The fellowship is Tolkien's Fellowship of the Ring in The Lord of the Rings.
explanation.definitionFit: Aragorn is one of the nine companions in the Fellowship of the Ring, the ranger who becomes king.

clue.text: King's dark time with criminal getting honour

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king; the 's links it to what follows
night is the dark part of the day
a hood, short for hoodlum, is a criminal

explanation.surface: A monarch suffers a dark period alongside a criminal, yet still receives an award.
explanation.definitionFit: A knighthood is a title conferred by the monarch, one of the classic British honours.

clue.text: Saying is edited to the greatest degree

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for a past participle: something maximised has been taken to the greatest degree

parts.note: a maxim is a saying
taken as written
ed. is the abbreviation for edited

explanation.surface: A proverb has been revised as thoroughly as possible.
explanation.definitionFit: To maximise is to increase something to its utmost, so a maximised quantity has been raised as far as it goes.

clue.text: Mishandles alarm test badly

indicators.note: something done badly comes out wrong, so the preceding letters are put in a disordered arrangement

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone botches a fire-alarm test.
explanation.definitionFit: To maltreat is to treat badly or abuse, which is a harsher form of mishandling.

clue.text: 6 across dissected with a twist: 'A line with a few values'

definitions.text: A line with a few values

indicators.note: twisting something round turns it end to end, so the whole string is read backwards

parts.note: the number written as a word
split into two, across becomes a cross: A plus X, the letter shaped like a cross

explanation.surface: It poses as a cross-reference to another clue, followed by a quoted description of a graph.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no 6 across in the grid: the 6 is the number SIX, and 'across' cut in two is 'a cross'. SIX A X reversed gives X-AXIS.
explanation.definitionFit: The x-axis of a graph is a horizontal line marked with a scale of values.

clue.text: Satisfied about a key component of discussion

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word is wrapped round the next

parts.note: a demand is met when it is satisfied
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is content with a central point raised in a debate.
explanation.definitionFit: The meat of an argument or discussion is its substance, the essential core.

clue.text: Succeeded? Success is hard and beastly

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in genealogies
a win is a success
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A cynical remark that achieving success is tough and brutal.
explanation.definitionFit: Swinish means like a pig, coarse or nasty, matching beastly as an insult.

clue.text: Incompetent constable to follow English food writer

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them
Mary Berry is an English cookery writer and television baker

explanation.surface: A police officer who can't do the job is told to shadow a celebrity cook.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogberry is the bumbling, word-mangling constable in Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing.

clue.text: Cold German and American spies coming in all out of sorts

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for German

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so the spies go inside the other letters

parts.note: the word all, rearranged; the spies go in after its first two letters

indicators.note: being out of sorts means being disordered, so the word before it is jumbled

parts.note: the CIA is the US intelligence agency

explanation.surface: A Cold War scene: German and American agents arriving in a state of disarray.
explanation.definitionFit: Glacial means icy, like a glacier, and is a strong word for cold, of weather or of manner.

clue.text: Offering assessment in hospital by seeking divine intervention? Not initially

indicators.note: not initially says the opening letter is dropped from the phrase it follows

parts.note: X is the multiplication sign, read as by, as in three by four
praying is asking God to intervene

explanation.surface: A hospital patient awaits an assessment, praying for a miracle.
explanation.walkthrough: PRAYING loses its first letter to RAYING; 'by' as X comes from dimensions such as 3 x 4.
explanation.definitionFit: X-raying a patient is a radiographic examination, a way of assessing injuries in hospital.

clue.text: Something for the nippers in addition: book probing childhood disease

parts.note: too means also, in addition

indicators.note: a probe goes inside, so the book letter is pushed into the disease

parts.note: thrush is a fungal infection common in babies' mouths
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: Something for small children, plus a book about a childhood illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nippers' looks like children, which the surface encourages, but here it means teeth, the things that nip.
explanation.definitionFit: A toothbrush cleans teeth, and teeth are jocularly the nippers because they bite.

clue.text: Interval in cup match enthralling millions

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so the match word holds the other letter inside

parts.note: a tie is a knockout cup match in football
M is the abbreviation for millions

explanation.surface: A half-time break in a cup game watched by millions of viewers.
explanation.definitionFit: A time is a period or interval, as in 'for a time'.

clue.text: Experienced worker troubled me on a jury, note

indicators.note: troubled means disturbed, so the following words are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
N is the abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: A seasoned worker is uneasy about serving on a jury and writes a note.
explanation.definitionFit: A journeyman is a trained, qualified tradesman working for an employer, a reliable experienced hand.

clue.text: A coin — the tossing is not determined

indicators.note: a tossed coin flips over and over, so these letters land in a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
also part of the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The result of a coin toss is uncertain until it lands.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'the tossing' as one phrase, but 'the' belongs with 'A coin' as letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Inchoate means just begun and not yet fully formed, so still undetermined.

clue.text: Young worker born ready to work

indicators.note: putting letters to work makes them do something new, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A youngster who was simply born for employment.
explanation.definitionFit: An errand boy is a lad employed to run errands and deliver messages, a classic junior job.

clue.text: Separate irritation, scratching head

indicators.note: scratching means striking out, and the head is the front, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: bother is annoyance or irritation

explanation.surface: Someone scratches their head over a distinct annoyance.
explanation.definitionFit: Other as an adjective means separate or distinct, as in 'the other house'.

clue.text: First couple from school walk and climb roughly

indicators.note: the first couple means the opening pair of letters of the next word

parts.note: the first two letters of school
a ramble is a leisurely walk

explanation.surface: A school's leading pair go walking and hill climbing.
explanation.definitionFit: To scramble is to climb or clamber over rough ground using hands as well as feet.

clue.text: Startled comment about doctor in group

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the exclamation goes round the medical letters

parts.note: coo! is a British exclamation of surprise
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise about a doctor who belongs to a band.
explanation.definitionFit: A combo is a small band of musicians, especially in jazz, so a group.

clue.text: Vehicle overturned during race — unexpectedly fortunate outcome?

indicators.note: during means in the course of, so the vehicle sits inside the race

parts.note: the mile is a running race

indicators.note: something overturned is upside down, so in a down entry the word is read bottom to top

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A car flips over during a motor race, yet everyone walks away unhurt.
explanation.definitionFit: A miracle is an extraordinary, welcome event, often an escape that seemed impossible.

clue.text: Drink, swallowing last of beer, and stand in shock

indicators.note: swallowing means taking inside, so the drink word holds the letter

parts.note: to sup is to drink

indicators.note: last of means only the final letter of the following word is used

parts.note: the final letter of beer
to rise is to stand up

explanation.surface: Someone takes a swig of beer and gets to their feet, aghast.
explanation.definitionFit: Surprise is the feeling of shock at something unexpected.

clue.text: Unhappy about shops creating promotional opportunity

indicators.note: about means around, so the mood word goes round the shops

parts.note: sad means unhappy
a mall is a complex of shops

explanation.surface: Someone gloomy about the local shops turns that into a marketing chance.
explanation.definitionFit: A small ad is a classified advertisement in a newspaper, a cheap way to promote something.

clue.text: Former king, say, repeatedly upset about soldiers

indicators.note: about means around, so the two copies enclose the soldiers
upset means knocked over, so in a down entry the word is turned bottom to top, and done twice

parts.note: e.g., for example, is what say means here, taken twice
OR, other ranks, are ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: A former monarch is described as repeatedly annoyed with his troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Six British kings have been called George, so the name fits any of those past monarchs.

clue.text: Emanation of the ear? Not quite

indicators.note: not quite means falling just short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: aural means relating to the ear

explanation.surface: A puzzled question whether some emission comes from the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: An aura is a subtle quality or glow felt to emanate from a person or thing.

clue.text: Result of baking: experts taken aback about smell; kitchen evacuated at first

indicators.note: about means around, so the reversed experts surround the smell
taken aback puns on being taken backwards, so the experts are read in reverse

parts.note: aces are experts
pong is British slang for a bad smell

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letters of the preceding words are used

parts.note: the first letters of kitchen and evacuated

explanation.surface: Experts are startled by a smell from the oven, and the kitchen is cleared at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken aback' looks like surprise, and 'kitchen evacuated' like an emergency; both are mechanics.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponge cake is a light cake produced by baking a whisked batter.

clue.text: Pointless climbing — without this?

indicators.note: letters that climb move about and shift position, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the first part of pointless, its letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A climber asks whether going up without this piece of gear would be futile.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as point-less: the letters of POINT, rearranged, are the thing climbing would be pointless without.
explanation.definitionFit: A piton is a metal peg hammered into rock to secure a rope, an essential piece of climbing protection.

clue.text: Potential entry in charts very much no good

parts.note: so means very much, as in 'so kind'
NG is the abbreviation for no good

explanation.surface: A grumble that a hopeful chart entry is really very poor.
explanation.definitionFit: The charts are the pop music sales rankings, so a song is something that could enter them.

clue.text: Evade second escape clause?

parts.note: to second a proposal is to back it
an out is a way of escape, such as a get-out clause

explanation.surface: A question whether a contract's second escape clause is a way to dodge obligations.
explanation.definitionFit: To back out of something is to withdraw from a commitment, avoiding it.

clue.text: Incompetent Dickens character — the end of Oliver?

definitions.note: an adjective for a noun: a bumbler is an incompetent person

parts.note: Mr Bumble is the pompous beadle in Dickens's Oliver Twist

indicators.note: the end of means only the final letter of the following word is taken

parts.note: the final letter of Oliver

explanation.surface: A question whether an inept Dickens figure brings about the end of Oliver Twist.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver looks like Oliver Twist the novel, Mr Bumble's home, but here it only supplies its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A bumbler is someone clumsy and inept, an incompetent in noun form.

clue.text: European forbearance about information in crisis

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European

indicators.note: about means around, so the forbearance word wraps round the information

parts.note: mercy is forbearance from punishment
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: A European shows restraint over information during a crisis.
explanation.definitionFit: An emergency is a sudden dangerous situation, which is what a crisis is.

clue.text: Encouragement not covered, needing involvement of Government

indicators.note: involvement means being drawn in, so one letter is placed inside the other word

parts.note: nude means uncovered
G is the abbreviation for government

explanation.surface: Encouragement that is not hidden needs government involvement.
explanation.definitionFit: A nudge is a gentle prod, and figuratively a bit of encouragement toward doing something.
